title: Introduction to MongoDB
subtitle: What MongoDB is, why NoSQL, and when to use it
author: KERNAL

whyItExists.problem: Relational databases require a fixed schema defined up front. When your data shape changes frequently—like user profiles with different attributes—you end up with many NULL columns, complex migrations, and rigid structure that slows development.
whyItExists.solution: MongoDB stores data as flexible JSON-like documents. Fields can vary between documents in the same collection. No schema migrations needed when you add new fields.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Use MongoDB for hierarchical data, catalogs with varying attributes, event logs, real-time analytics, content management, and applications where the data model evolves rapidly.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Avoid MongoDB when you need complex multi-table transactions, strict relational integrity (foreign keys enforced by the database), or when your team is already expert in SQL and the data is naturally tabular.

explainModes.beginner: MongoDB is a database where instead of rows in a spreadsheet, you store JSON objects. Each object can have different fields, so a user profile can have a 'phone' field while another doesn't, and MongoDB is fine with that.
explainModes.simple: MongoDB is a NoSQL document database. It stores data as BSON documents (like JSON) in collections (like tables). No fixed schema means flexible, evolving data structures.
explainModes.standard: MongoDB is a document-oriented database that stores BSON documents in schema-free collections. It supports horizontal scaling, rich queries, secondary indexes, and an aggregation pipeline. It trades some relational features for flexibility and performance at scale.
explainModes.technical: MongoDB uses a document model backed by BSON (Binary JSON) with 16MB document size limit. Data is stored in WiredTiger storage engine with collection-level locking in older versions and document-level locking since 3.x. It supports ACID transactions since 4.0 (multi-document), and provides replication via replica sets and sharding for horizontal scale-out.
explainModes.deepDive: MongoDB's WiredTiger storage engine uses a B-tree structure with snappy/zlib/zstd compression. BSON encoding allows O(1) field access by offset. The oplog (operations log) in replica sets records all mutations as idempotent operations, enabling both replication and change streams. Transactions use a multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) model with snapshot isolation at the session level.

content.text: MongoDB is a document-oriented NoSQL database that stores data as flexible JSON-like documents called BSON. Unlike relational databases, MongoDB collections do not enforce a fixed schema — each document can have different fields and data types.

Founded in 2009, MongoDB is now one of the most popular databases in the world, used by companies like Adobe, eBay, LinkedIn, and Uber. It excels at storing hierarchical, unstructured, or semi-structured data that doesn't fit neatly into rows and columns.

a.name: MongoDB (NoSQL)
strengths: Flexible schema — fields vary per document
Native JSON support — no ORM needed
weaknesses: Not ideal for complex multi-table transactions
a.useWhen: Data varies in shape, you need to scale out, or you are building a catalog, CMS, or real-time feed

b.name: SQL (Relational)
weaknesses: Rigid schema — migrations required for changes
b.useWhen: Data is naturally tabular, you need strict consistency, or complex multi-table reporting

content.definition: A JSON-like record stored in MongoDB. Equivalent to a row in SQL but with no fixed columns. Documents are stored as BSON (Binary JSON) internally.
A group of documents, like a SQL table but schema-free. All documents in a collection are related by convention, not enforced by the database.
A container for collections. One MongoDB server can host many databases, each completely isolated.

content.text: MongoDB auto-creates a collection when you first insert into it. You don't need to define the schema before writing data — perfect for rapid prototyping.

MongoDB stores documents in BSON (Binary JSON), which extends JSON with additional types like Date, ObjectId, Binary, Decimal128, and regular expressions. This makes MongoDB more precise than plain JSON for data storage.

questions.question: What is a MongoDB document?
options: A table row with fixed columns
A JSON-like record with flexible fields
questions.explanation: MongoDB documents are flexible JSON-like records stored as BSON. They do not require a fixed schema — different documents in the same collection can have different fields.

questions.question: What is the MongoDB equivalent of a SQL table?
questions.explanation: A Collection in MongoDB is equivalent to a SQL table — it holds a group of related documents.

questions.question: Which of the following is a valid reason to choose MongoDB over a relational database?
options: You need enforced foreign key constraints
Your data has a highly variable schema that changes often
questions.explanation: MongoDB shines when your data schema changes frequently or varies per record. For enforced foreign keys and complex joins, SQL is the better choice.

faq.q: When should I use MongoDB over SQL?
faq.a: MongoDB excels when your data is hierarchical or when the schema changes frequently. Use it for product catalogs, user profiles, event logs, and content management. Use SQL for complex joins, enforced relational integrity, and strict ACID transactions across multiple tables.

MongoDB is schema-flexible by default, but you can enforce a schema using JSON Schema validation rules on a collection. In practice, most teams define an implicit schema through their application code or use Mongoose to enforce it at the ODM layer.
Yes. Since MongoDB 4.0, multi-document ACID transactions are supported. Single-document operations have always been atomic. For most use cases, single-document atomicity is sufficient.

usedIn: Mobile app backends (user profiles, activity feeds)
examples: Storing user profiles with varying attributes — one user has 'bio', another has 'company', no schema change needed
Logging app events with different schemas per event type (page_view, purchase, error)
Building a product catalog where electronics have 'specs.RAM' and clothing has 'specs.size'
